Hey hey! Looks like nobody answered, which is a shame. I'm more accustomed to answering "Why is Philosophy Useful?", so my response is going to be through that lens working backwards in a way.

I would say first and foremost is that philosophy is the use of a certain set of tools in order to construct a hypothesis, theory, or experiment (thought or otherwise) to:

  • Demonstrate how a thing in the World (capital W intended) works.

  • Provoke a meaningful discussion about "a thing in the World".

  • Provide a guide or framework for exploring or studying "a thing in the World".

I'm ignoring a lot of academic rigor for the sake of brevity - each of those categories have a certain academic gravity that I'm happy to discuss or develop further if need be, but I'm going to stick to those for now.

The primary tool used is going to be logic to examine and determine the strength of an assertion, but something that I think gets glossed over all-too frequently is gut instinct. I don't think gut instinct carries a lot of weight on its own, however if something unsettles you, or disagrees with you, it would be dishonest to yourself not to explore why that is using logic and your current understanding.

Philosophy provides often-ignored guideposts. My particular interests and training lie in analytical philosophies - using our understanding of science to create metastudies and provide testable hypotheses. I love reading about existentialism, because you can learn so much about how people view themselves, the world, and their place in it just by what authors resonate with them, or what parts of theories to which they subscribe or enjoy, even if it's not a formalized theory.

Philosophy, much like any other discipline, gives you a set of tools and instructions on how to use them then sets you out into the world to see what you bring back or make of it. It does not judge, but it does test. There is competition in and among every school of thought, but everyone is a colleague trying to learn and propose something new about the world. I think it's beautiful that way, even though a lot of people try to dismiss it as nothing more than constant pondering and harumphing in an ivory tower somewhere.

Not OP, but I found your post rather helpful. I'm looking into philosophy myself, currently reading Beyond Good and Evil and seeing how I feel about that.

Any recommendations for a philosophical noob?

I have a few! I've been out of the game for a little bit, but hopefully these will be useful:

Existentialism by Solomon is a great way to get involved in some kind of "best of" passages for existentialism. It takes out a lot of the time spent on establishing frameworks and giving you most of the gist of stuff. If you get hung up on Heidegger, don't worry, so does everyone else.

To get into the broader scheme of the Philosophy of Science, I believe this is the book we used when I was in undergrad.

And if you like Philosophy of Science, then one of the subcategories (Philosophy of the Mind) is super interesting! I haven't been able to read much on this one, but I hear good things Philosophy of the Mind by Kim sounds like a good primer for more advanced books like one of my faves The Conscious Brain by Prinz.

My focuses are lightly in existentialism, but primarily in PoS/M. Thus Spake Zarathustra is pretty fun to read, but some Hegel digests are always fun to start with then branching on out to others.

I do have a soft spot for classic philosophers (Marcus Aurelius ftw), so check out some nice poetic translations, because preserving the verse form factor I think provides a certain relevance to what they're saying and provides additional subtext.

Hopefully that's a good start!

Hello, Voat!

We're doing a project for our school which aims to spread awareness for Tinnitus. As you can imagine, there are PLENTY of young people in college who seem to detest their own hearing. Blaring Hip-Hop and pop in their earbuds, forever damaging their ever-so-delicate hearing nerves not knowing the risk they're taking. Anyway, we're planning on raising a bit of money and then spread the good word about what entails Tinnitus, how bad it is, the stigma around it, what's been tried, and what is on the pipeline as far as treatment goes.

We're in the process of establishing media accounts on Tumblr, Youtube, Google+, Reddit, Instagram, Facebook, and Vine. We're also establishing partnerships with the local Veteran Administration clinic, chiropractors, a few ENTs, and the local school's Tinnitus clinic.

Finally, the reason why we're here: we're trying to come up with a way to get young adult's attention on the issue. After trying the regular ways (bake sales, flyers, etc), we're ready to try new things. For example, we were thinking of walking around with tone generators set to high frequencies for short amount of times. Frequencies which can only be heard by young people so that the older individuals won't be bothered. We cleared with a few people, and this is no different than blasting music when in public.

Are there any other subtle yet disruptive ideas that anyone else care to share? If we do make it to first place, we could be featured in the school newspaper and perhaps locally as well. No promises though.
